title: More real guns
notes: Real 3D models (public domain) for the Colt M4, the AKM and the Remington 870, plus the grenades in your hand and in the air.

New real guns at real prices: the Remington 700 SPS with a 3-9× scope (,100; aim to look through it), the Makarov PM (50, in its own 9×18mm), the Luger P08 (,800, a collector piece), and two WWII submachine guns at what registered machine guns really sell for: the M3A1 Grease Gun (4,000) and the Suomi KP/-31 with its 71-round drum (6,000).
On the model guns the magazine really comes out when you reload, and the shotgun fore-end really slides when you pump it.
People (real soldier models and motion-captured animation) are next.

title: Real 3D models
notes: Real 3D models (Poly Haven, public domain), scanned and modelled from the real things:

Two real guns: the Walther P1 (P38) is a new pistol (50), and the sniper slot is now the real Mosin–Nagant M91/30 PU with its 3.5× scope, in its real 7.62×54R calibre (00). Aim to look through the PU scope. Its shot is the actual Mosin recording.
The machete and a new camp hatchet (replacing the tomahawk) are real models too.

The maps are full of real objects: oil drums, old tyres, military crates and ammo boxes at the checkpoints, jerrycans, gas bottles, cement bags and generators by the houses, boxes and plastic crates at the market, dumpsters, utility cabinets, concrete road barriers, wall-mounted AC units, scrub, and cars under tarps. They load in the background (about 9 MB, once), simplified so they cost little to draw; Low keeps the light stand-ins.

title: Real surfaces
notes: Photo-scanned surfaces (Poly Haven, public domain) on Medium and up: real plaster on the houses, real sand underfoot, cracked asphalt at the port, concrete, cinder blocks, weathered planks, corrugated and rusted iron, steel plate. Each has real bumps, roughness and dirt in the creases, so the light catches them properly.
The shipping containers keep their colours and company names but get the dents, ribs and wear of a real container.
They load in the background (about 5 MB, once); Low keeps the light drawn textures.
If the game is slow: check the red banner on the title screen. In Edge, graphics acceleration had been switched off, which makes any browser game run on the processor instead of the graphics card.

title: Is your graphics card being used?
notes: If the browser is drawing the game without your graphics card (hardware acceleration switched off), the title screen now shows a red banner that stays, with how to turn it back on. That alone can make the game many times faster.
The F3 readout shows the graphics chip on its own line (it was being cut off), and flags software drawing in red.
Changing the graphics setting during a match prepares the new shaders straight away, instead of stuttering.

title: A much lighter Low
notes: Low now uses simpler lighting on every surface, a plain sky (the realistic sky is costly on every sky pixel) and no clouds. About twice the frame rate on Low.
When the game can't keep up, it now lowers its resolution further (down to half).
New: press F3 (or Settings > Show FPS) for frames per second, frame time, draw calls, resolution and which graphics chip is drawing the game.
If your browser is drawing the game without your graphics card (hardware acceleration switched off), the title screen now tells you how to fix it.

title: Smooth on PC, playable on phones
notes: Much smoother: the stutters are gone. Gun models are built once and copied (a gun appearing used to freeze the game for a moment), soldiers share their body meshes, bot path-finding is several times faster and spread out, textures no longer stall the graphics card, and every shader is compiled while the match loads instead of mid-fight.

Low is now properly light: no shadows, no anti-aliasing, a shorter view distance. Medium redraws shadows every other frame. Shadows only cover the area around you, and far-away soldiers do not cast them.
New players start on Medium (phones on Low). Anti-aliasing changes after a reload.

Phones: on-screen controls. A stick wherever your left thumb lands, drag the right side to look, and buttons for fire, aim, reload, jump, crouch, sprint, swap, melee, throw (and grenade type), first aid, buy, scores, fire mode, light and pause. A TAKE GUN button pops up by dropped guns.

Phones get gentle aim assist (stronger while aiming), fullscreen landscape when you deploy, a smaller HUD and menus that fit, and a reminder to turn the phone sideways. Phones and PCs play in the same matches.

title: Graphics, guns, soldiers and feel
notes: A real sky: physically based scattering, drifting clouds, and light from the sky on everything (metal and plastic now reflect it).

Post-processing: colour grading, vignette, film grain and lens fringing; bloom on muzzle flashes and explosions (High); ambient occlusion for soft contact shadows (new Ultra setting). Being hurt drains the colour and darkens the edges; rounds snapping past smear the edges of your view.

Guns rebuilt with rounded parts and real detail: rail teeth, M-LOK slots, charging handles, ejection ports, forward assists, triggers and guards, ribbed magazines, slide serrations, scope rings, sling swivels.

Soldiers rebuilt: rounded bodies with faces and ears, plate carriers with cummerbunds, loaded magazine pouches, radios, hydration packs, a holstered pistol, cargo pockets, knee pads and proper boots; helmets with rails, NVG mounts and chin straps.
Better animation: legs step the way you are actually moving when strafing or backing up, the body leans into a sprint, hips sway, soldiers breathe when standing still.

The maps are lived in: window frames and sills, painted shutters and open doors, water tanks and satellite dishes on the roofs, AC units on the walls, oil drums, tyres, rubble, dry scrub, rubbish, better palm trees; at the port, jersey barriers, pallet stacks, cable reels, puddles and lane markings.
Effects: a 3D muzzle flash, glowing tracers, chips of plaster, wood and concrete that fly off walls and bounce, and explosions with a fireball, a shockwave ring, flying dirt and a column of smoke.
Feel: recoil kicks and springs back, a short camera punch per shot, the gun rolls as you strafe and dips when you land.
Faster despite all that: whole soldiers, guns and scenery are merged into a few draw calls each. Low and Medium stay light for weaker PCs.

title: Real gunshots
notes: Every gun now fires real recordings (from the CC0 Free Firearm Sound Library): AR-15, AK-47 and SKS, a .30-06 Tikka for the battle rifles, Springfield 1917 and Mosin Nagant for the snipers, three real 12-gauge pump guns, Walther PPQ, Colt 1911, a .38 revolver and a Swedish K submachine gun.
Gunfire far away uses recordings made at a distance, so a firefight across the map sounds like one: duller, with the echo coming back off the buildings.
The .50 BMG and .50 AE use those recordings pitched down. Reloads, impacts and explosions are still synthesized for now.

title: COLD BORE
notes: A realistic online multiplayer FPS: Free-for-all, Team Deathmatch and Domination on two maps (Al-Hadra, a desert town, and Kessel Freight Yard, a container port).
Quick Play finds an online match; if there isn't one, you host one and bots fill the empty places. Bots leave as real players join. Server browser, private matches with a code, and offline vs bots.

27 real guns at their real prices (a Glock 17 is $550, an M4 $1,150, a Barrett M82 $9,500), real attachments (EOTech, ACOG, suppressors with the $200 tax stamp), melee weapons, grenades, first aid and armour. Kills pay $500 (+$250 headshot) and the money is yours for the match.
Ballistics: bullet drop, travel time, penetration through walls and bodies, armour levels IIIA / III / IV and helmets that stop what they would really stop.
Wounds where the rounds land, bleeding you have to treat (bandage, tourniquet, IFAK), limping on a leg hit, shaking aim on an arm hit. Ragdolls. Realistic gore with a slider from 0 (none) to 100.
Your bank (every dollar you earn) buys uniforms and Cerakote finishes in the Armory. Controllers (Xbox, PlayStation, Steam Deck), installable as an app.
